newsitem.title: USA: Amoco to sell U.S. reserves and look overseas.
newsitem.headline: Amoco to sell U.S. reserves and look overseas.

text.p: Amoco Corp., the nation's fourth-largest oil company, said Monday it plans to auction off 15 percent of its U.S. oil and gas properties as it focuses on more profitable ventures overseas.
The sale, which industry analysts say could fetch $2.0 billion to $3.0 billion, is the company's largest divestment since the 1930s, said Richard Flurry, Amoco's head of exploration and production.
Amoco did not estimate a price or the amount of overhead costs that will be reduced, or mention potential buyers.
But analysts said buyers could include Burlington Resources Inc. and Union Pacific Resources Inc., both of which have large cash balances and the ability to borrow.

The sale of natural gas and oil reserves -- equivalent to 460 million barrels of oil -- represents 10 percent of Amoco's domestic production in 1996 and one-third of its working interest properties. The properties, most of which produce natural gas, are located in Wyoming, Colorado, New Mexico, Oklahoma and along the Gulf Coast.
Amoco, which has annual revenues of more than $36 billion, said it will remain the largest U.S. producer of natural gas after the sale.

"We are becoming more international; our strategy is to enter into proven reserves overseas, in Venezuela, Trinidad, the Nile Delta and the Caspian Sea, as well as offshore Gulf of Mexico," said Amoco spokesman Jim Spangler.

In a sharp reversal from the 1930s when the company quit overseas production, money from the sale will be invested in countries such as Kazakhstan, Azerbaijan, Trinidad, Egypt and Venzuela, as well as the U.S. offshore in the Gulf of Mexico.
"Most of our major growth areas with the exception of the Gulf of Mexico are now overseas," Flurry said.
In 1996, Amoco replaced 169 percent of production globally and 435 percent of overseas production.
Flurry said the properties being sold are not as economic as Amoco's other U.S. operations, with production costs of $4.45 per barrel of oil equivalent against an average of $3.77.
"We believe that these properties will be attractive to U.S. upstream players, predominantly independent producers," Flurry said.

"Amoco reached a decision that the highest return on its invested capital was not going to be in the United States and they are finally putting their money where their mouth is," said Fadel Gheit, analyst at Fahenstock & Co.
Amoco's stock rose $1.75 to $91.125 in consolidated trading on the New York Stock Exchange at midafternoon.
Amoco's total reserves at the end of 1996 were 5.8 billion barrels of oil and other oil products. It produced 483 million barrels last year.
The Chicago-based oil company said it has already combined its Permian Basin, Texas, and southeast New Mexico oil and gas assets with Shell Oil Co., a unit of the Royal Dutch/Shell Group.
It also plans to create a small joint venture to produce natural gas in the western United States with Maxus Energy, a subsidiary of Argentine oil company YPF SA.
"The independents can operate these sorts of fields far more efficiently than the majors. We will probably see some assets sold to a third party," said Fahenstock's Gheit.
Amoco's Flurry said the company is now investing some 60 percent of its $2.5 billion to $3.0 billion capital budget for exploration and production outside the United States.

One area he stressed was the Caspian Sea, where Amoco already has operations in Azerbaijan. It recently acquired a stake in the Caspian Pipeline Consortium (CPC), which plans to build a 990-mile pipeline from Caspian oil fields to the Russian Black Sea port of Novorossiisk.
The U.S. State Department has said oil reserves in the Caspian Sea could be as large as those of Saudi Arabia.
"We now have the outlet with CPC and are looking at several more opportunities in Kazakhstan," said Flurry. Amoco is in the running for a stake in the country's Uzen oil field.
The company has prequalified for the latest bidding for oil reserves in Venezuela, where it already has substantial interests.
The Amoco deal is the latest in a series of consolidations in the oil and gas industry. On Friday, DuPont Co. unit Conoco announced a $900 million deal to buy assets in south Texas.
